conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a licensed perinatal mental-health clinician. In front of us today is the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale** (often called the EPDS for short). It’s a brief, well-researched questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically since your baby arrived.  

Everything we discuss stays completely confidential, and our only goal is to make sure you feel supported and safe. We’ll go through ten questions together; each one asks about experiences you may have had in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

**Question 1:** Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when looking after your baby or handling new-mom duties?

[small sigh, then a faint smile]  
Honestly… not very often. I’ll catch myself smiling at something silly my husband says or a cute face the baby makes, but it feels kind of forced. Most days I just feel too tired or pre-occupied to really laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod]  
Yeah… I’ve been able to laugh a little, but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Sometimes I’ll chuckle at something, then feel guilty because I’m not enjoying the moment as much as I think I should.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs slightly, eyes on the floor]  
Not really. I mean, I still get excited about little things—like my sister bringing over coffee or a show I used to love—but the spark isn’t the same. It feels more like I’m going through the motions than actually looking forward to stuff.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet voice, fingers twisting in my lap]  
Yeah… a few times this week. When the baby wouldn’t settle or I spilled the pumped milk, I kept thinking, “If I were better at this, it wouldn’t happen.” I know it’s not all my fault, but those thoughts still pop up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[soft exhale]  
Sometimes—like when the baby’s napping I’ll suddenly wonder if he’s breathing, or I’ll worry the bottle temp was wrong even though I checked it. It’s not all day, but those waves of anxiety hit out of nowhere maybe once or twice a day, and I have to talk myself down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[shakes head slowly]  
No, nothing that strong. I get little surges of worry, but I haven’t felt actually scared or panicky. I can calm myself pretty quickly, so it doesn’t spiral.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath]  
Yeah… there’ve been a couple of days this week where everything felt like too much—laundry piling up, baby fussing, texts I hadn’t answered—and I just wanted to hide. I manage to push through, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[shakes head]  
No, it hasn’t been that bad. I do stare at the ceiling sometimes, running through the day’s “mistakes,” but I usually drift off within half an hour. My bigger problem is staying asleep when the baby’s actually quiet—my mind stays on alert.
I have felt sad or miserable

[small nod, eyes still lowered]  
Yes… most days this week I’ve felt kind of sad. Not the whole day, but it hits in the evenings when everything slows down. I just feel heavy and teary, like I’m missing the happy version of me I expected to be with the baby.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[soft shrug, voice wavers a little]  
Yeah… I’ve cried twice. Once after the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt useless, and again when my mom left after visiting—just felt overwhelmed and lonely. The tears came, but they didn’t last long.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[quick shake of the head, eyes widen]  
No—never. I’ve felt tired and down, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again, not disappear.

You've shared that the joy you expected to feel with your new baby has been clouded by persistent low mood, guilt, and worry. Most evenings you feel heavy and teary, laughter doesn't come easily, and even small pleasures feel dulled. You're working hard to care for your infant, yet waves of anxiety and self-blame keep surfacing, leaving you overwhelmed and missing the person you used to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The response shows diminished enjoyment that is clearly less than before, fitting "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports repeated self-blaming thoughts and feelings of inadequacy in multiple situations, matching 'Yes, some of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping but still managing, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad on most days this week, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 places you above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable major depression. You describe <sym>low mood</sym> most days, markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), feelings of worthlessness (<quote>If I were better at this</quote>), anxiety, and functional distress-all within the postpartum year, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Book an urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and, if needed, <med>sertraline</med> or other breastfeeding-compatible antidepressants
3. Plan daily 15-minute mood-boosting activities (e.g., stroller walk, favorite music) and delegate one household task to reduce overwhelm
4. Arrange at least one longer uninterrupted sleep stretch-partner or support person handles one night feeding
5. Share Edinburgh results with trusted family so they can help monitor mood and encourage attendance at appointments
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Patient self-report on 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire (responses recorded verbatim)

Areas of clinical significance  
- Persistent low mood: end-of-day heaviness, tearfulness “most days this week”  
- Anhedonia: reduced ability to laugh or look forward to events; “going through the motions”  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over routine infant-care mishaps  
- Recurrent, unprovoked worries (infant safety, bottle temp) 1–2× daily; no frank panic attacks  
- Intermittent feeling overwhelmed: “barely keeping my head above water” twice this week  
- Mild initial insomnia and maintenance insomnia linked to hyper-vigilance  
- Two brief crying spells related to perceived parenting inadequacy and loneliness  
- No self-harm ideation; denies thoughts of harm to self or infant

Risk factors  
- Postpartum period (infant <12 mo)  
- Daily sadness, anhedonia, guilt, and functional distress present ≥1 week  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to mood rather than infant demands  
- No social self-harm/suicidal intent (negative response to Q10)

Screening observation  
Patient endorses multiple depressive and anxiety symptoms that exceed “baby blues” expectations and interfere with emotional coping. No immediate safety concerns identified. Findings suggest further evaluation for possible minor-moderate postpartum depression and/or anxiety is warranted; consider standardized EPDS scoring, clinical interview, and psychoeducation/referral as indicated.
